Phantom Advantages: why a “good” world-model representation is a bad initialization for sparse-reward RL

An automated-research dive into experiment 010 (real LS20 Level 1, terminal-only reward). All artifacts in exp_010_ls20_cnn_ppo_jepa/exp_010_3/. Single seed unless noted; key results replicated over 3 seeds.
Abstract. On the real LS20 game a vanilla CNN+PPO agent with a randomly-initialized encoder reliably solves Level 1 under terminal-only reward, yet warm-starting the same agent from a JEPA world-model encoder — pretrained to predict the environment’s own dynamics — drops success to 0%. The intuitive culprit (the JEPA features are “bad”/mis-scaled) is wrong: we falsify three such hypotheses in turn (feature content, feature norm, encoder drift). The real cause is a single, simple mechanism we call the phantom-advantage trap. Under terminal-only reward, before the first success there is no task signal, so the only gradient acting on the policy comes through the value critic. An informative encoder gives the critic enough expressive power to fit its own approximation noise into a state-structured value function V(s); GAE + advantage-normalization convert that structure into persistent, state-consistent phantom advantages; PPO “exploits” them and collapses the exploratory policy — entropy falls even though the agent has never seen a reward — so the rare goal is never stumbled upon. A random encoder — whose features are dominated by a large state-invariant component (only ~1% of the feature norm varies across states; note they are not low-rank — mean-centered, their pairwise cosine is ≈0 just like JEPA’s) — yields V(s)≈const, so the critic fits V≈0 immediately, no phantom advantages arise, and its policy stays a stable explorer and finds the reward. We confirm the mechanism causally: deleting the value baseline (Monte-Carlo advantages) rescues the JEPA encoder, which then solves at every seed (u≈21–34). Finally we show the deeper tension: in a frozen-encoder probe the JEPA representation is the more transferable one to Level 2 (it preserves forward-dynamics structure that the task-specific PPO encoder discards) — i.e. the very richness that makes a representation transferable is what makes it sabotage sparse-reward exploration.

1 · The phenomenon

Three variants share an identical architecture, PPO recipe, and seed; only the encoder treatment differs (system card §2). 10_0 trains the CNN from scratch; 10_1 adds an online JEPA(+IDM) loss to the shared encoder; 10_2 initializes the encoder from a JEPA model pretrained on random-policy data, then fine-tunes with PPO. Only 10_0 ever clears the level.

Note on “frozen” — two different experiments. The table’s “JEPA, frozen” row is a full 140-update PPO training run (encoder frozen, but the policy and value heads are trained); it fails. The H1 evidence below instead comes from a critic-free coverage rollout: the untrained, never-updated initial policy just sampling actions (no PPO, no value head in the loop). These probe different things — representational capacity vs optimization dynamics — so they do not contradict.

(H1) “The JEPA features are bad / capture the wrong latents.” Falsified by the critic-free coverage rollout: the untrained initial policy on the frozen JEPA encoder visits about the same number of distinct states as on the random encoder (~100–120) and still reaches the goal occasionally — so the features can represent and reach the goal; they are not incapable. (The “JEPA, frozen” training row fails for a different reason — its trainable critic still hallucinates advantages over the frozen features — which is evidence for the §3 mechanism, not for H1.) (H2) “The 66× feature-norm mismatch mis-calibrates the value head and floods the encoder with gradients.” This was even baked into the repo’s analyze_runs.py. Falsified: rescaling the JEPA features to the random-init norm makes the run perfectly “quiet” (grad 0.10, value-loss 0.001) yet it still never succeeds, and its entropy still slides down. (H3) “A trainable structured encoder drifts under value-fitting.” Falsified: freezing the encoder doesn’t help either. The common thread of all three failures: the encoder is informative (feature-cosine ≈ 0.6, not the random encoder’s ≈0.99), and entropy collapses with zero reward ever seen.

3 · The mechanism: the phantom-advantage trap

Reading guide / definitions.
  • zero-reward update — a PPO update on a rollout in which no success occurred, so every reward is 0; the only thing driving the actor is the critic.
  • entropy lost in one update (Fig 3c) — start from the untrained policy, do one zero-reward PPO update, measure the drop in mean action entropy. Isolates what the critic alone does to exploration in a single step.
  • advantage normalization — PPO replaces the advantages in each minibatch by their z-score, Â ← (Â − mean)/(std+ε). Mean-subtraction kills a constant advantage; dividing by std rescales whatever pattern remains to unit size, so a tiny-but-structured signal is amplified to the same influence as a large one — only the shape (which states/actions are above average) matters, not the magnitude.
  • state-consistent — the advantage is a reproducible function of (state,action), not per-sample noise, so its push on the policy does not average to zero across samples/updates. Evidence: the monotone entropy decline in Fig 2 (noise would random-walk, not steadily fall), and a positive split-half policy-gradient cosine (gradients computed on two disjoint halves of a zero-reward rollout agree: ~0.48 for JEPA vs ~0.33 for random).
  • “resc” / norm-matched — the JEPA encoder with its output rescaled to the random encoder’s feature norm. It is not the “rescue” run (that is resc_nobase in Fig 2, the no-critic variant).

The PPO actor gradient is E[ ∇log π(a|s) · Â ]: the reward never enters the actor directly — only through the advantage Â_t = Σ (γλ)^l δ_{t+l}, with δ_t = r_t + γV(s_{t+1}) − V(s_t) (and through having trained the critic, which itself touches the actor only via Â). With terminal-only reward and no success yet, every r_t = 0, so the advantage collapses to a pure function of the critic: Â_t = Σ (γλ)^l (γV(s_{t+1+l}) − V(s_{t+l})) — the whole actor gradient is now built from value differences with zero reward content (hence “phantom”). This does not vanish because the reward is 0; it vanishes only when V(s) is state-independent, for two reasons: (i) PPO normalizes advantages by subtracting the batch mean (ppo.py), so a constant V → constant δ → constant Â → ≈0; and (ii) the score function has zero mean, E[∇log π(a|s)]=0, so a state-independent advantage produces no consistent update regardless. When V(s) varies across states, Â becomes state-(and action-)correlated, survives normalization, and the policy reliably climbs the critic’s spurious value landscape: it exploits pure value-function noise. What sets V(s)’s expressiveness is the state-varying fraction of the (raw, pre-head) features: for the random encoder only ~1% of the feature norm varies across states (V_std≈0.02), so the critic drives V→0 almost instantly and no phantom signal persists; for the JEPA encoder ~11% varies (V_std≈5.5), giving the critic a real state-structured target it fits and re-generates over many updates. (This is not a rank/“collapse” distinction — mean-centered, both encoders’ features are full-rank; it is purely how large the state-dependent component is relative to a common state-invariant one.)

3.1 · Does the phantom advantage actually shape the policy? (direct evidence)

Fig 5 shows the source (V varies for JEPA, not random). Fig 6 closes the loop to the consequence. The chain, in the simplest 1-step terms: with r=0, the advantage of action a in state s is Â(s,a) ∝ γV(s′) − V(s). If neighbouring states have different value (JEPA: V_std 5.2), some actions get a systematically positive Â and are reinforced; if V≈const (random), no action is preferentially reinforced. We run 25 zero-reward updates (no success occurs) and, on a fixed probe set, watch the policy; from each rollout we log the whole-batch-normalized advantage broken down by action — the literal scalar that multiplies ∇log π.

Marginal bias vs state-dependence — the metric that really separates them. The marginal KL in Fig 6b looks almost the same for random and norm-matched JEPA, which seems to undercut the story. It doesn’t — KL(marginal‖uniform) only measures a global action bias and is blind to state-conditional shaping (per-state preferences that cancel in the average). Decompose the per-state entropy exactly: mean_s H(π(·|s)) = log4 − KL(π̄‖uniform) − I(S;A), where I(S;A) is the state–action mutual information = how state-dependent the policy became.

encoderper-state entropyKL(marginal‖uniform)I(S;A) — state-dependence
random1.2530.1330.000
JEPA (raw)1.0000.2160.170
JEPA (norm-matched)1.1090.1490.128

random and norm-matched JEPA have nearly equal marginal KL (0.133 vs 0.149), but their state-dependence differs categorically: I(S;A)=0.000 for random vs 0.128 for JEPA (≈ raw’s 0.170). random’s drift is a harmless uniform “biased coin” applied identically in every state — it does not change where exploration goes. The JEPA-driven phantom advantage instead makes the policy genuinely state-dependent — different states pushed toward different actions — bending the random walk into a state-conditioned path that gets trapped away from the goal. That state-conditional structure is exactly what the marginal KL cannot see, and it is the real signature of the phantom-advantage trap.

Where does the difference live, before vs after PPO’s advantage normalization? A natural worry is that normalization should wash the phantom out. Fig 8 traces the GAE advantage itself through normalization. (a) The raw advantage scale differs ~250× (std 0.023 random, 5.6 JEPA-raw). (b) After normalization (mean 0, std 1 for everyone), the marginal distributions are ~identical — and, checked over 8 seeds, even the higher moments don’t robustly differ (skew/kurtosis ≈ 0 for all; the per-seed skew we first saw was noise). So normalization erases not just the scale but the marginal shape too — the difference is genuinely not in the advantage’s marginal distribution. (c) What it cannot erase is the state-conditional structure: the same I(S;A) as above (0.000 random vs 0.128/0.170 JEPA). Conclusion: normalization removes everything except the dependence of the advantage on the state — and that residual is precisely what reshapes the policy. The phantom survives normalization as structure, not as a fatter histogram.

3.3 · The actual mechanism: credit generalization, not advantage value

A natural objection: at a given state s the advantage value is the same for both encoders (Fig 8b), so how can the representation change what gets reinforced? Because the policy is π(a|s)=softmax(W·h(s)): a gradient step that reinforces action a at s changes π(a|s′) at every other state s′ by an amount set by how similar h(s′) is to h(s). The advantage at s is identical; what differs is how the update generalizes to other states. Fig 9 measures this directly (matched feature norm): reinforce one action at one state, then look at the induced Δπ everywhere as a function of representational similarity.

This resolves the mechanism precisely. Pre-reward: the critic’s state-correlated phantom advantage, generalized through a localizing (JEPA) representation, writes state-specific action biases → it bends the exploratory walk into a trapped, state-conditioned path. Through a smearing (random) representation the same phantom can only shift the global policy — a harmless biased coin — so undirected coverage survives. Post-reward exploitation is the mirror image: localized credit assignment is exactly what you want to reproduce a winning trajectory. We tested it (script 13): behavior-cloning the 13-step winning L1 trajectory into a fresh head on a frozen encoder, both random and JEPA reproduce it and solve on replay — on L1 the states are already separable enough (random features are full-rank) that the representation gives no exploitation advantage. So on L1 the representation’s effect is confined to the pre-reward exploration phase. On the harder level (L2) it is not.

On L2, the JEPA representation beats random (exploitation). We replayed the 60-action Go-Explore L2 solution to get a winning trajectory (all 60 frames pixel-distinct, but only 49 distinct once the step-counter UI rows are masked → ~11 frames share player-state), and behavior-cloned it into a fresh head on each frozen encoder (5 head-init seeds). Frozen JEPA: BC acc 1.000, reproduces the win 5/5. Frozen random: BC acc 0.900, 0/5 — it cannot linearly separate the ~6 near-collinear states the win needs, so greedy replay diverges. (With a trainable encoder both solve.) So when the task requires distinguishing subtly-different states, JEPA’s structured representation is the deciding factor — the same localizing property that traps it pre-reward pays off for credit assignment once a reward exists.

3.4 · Why the random encoder works: cancellation pre-reward, differentiation post-reward

The policy-head gradient is Σ_t Â_t (π(·|s_t) − e_{a_t}) ⊗ h(s_t). Write h(s)=h̄+δ(s) (a big shared component + a small state-varying part). It splits into a marginal push (the h̄ part, a global shift of all logits) and a state-specific push (the δ(s) part). For the random encoder pre-reward, Â is sign-balanced noise: the marginal push averages to ≈0 (mean-zero advantage), and the state-specific push needs Â to correlate with δ(s) — which it doesn’t (V≈const), so it also averages to ≈0. Both terms cancel across states → the policy stays uniform. This is exactly the cancellation intuition, and it is what I(S;A)=0.000 measures. For JEPA, Â (built from V=w·h) is correlated with δ(s), so the state-specific term does not cancel → state-dependence emerges with no reward (I(S;A)=0.128) — the phantom.

What breaks the cancellation? A real reward. Once a success is sampled, the advantage acquires a consistent, reward-correlated component (the states/actions on the path to the goal), no longer noise. That component does not cancel — it backpropagates through the head into the encoder and amplifies the features δ(s) that separate reward-relevant states. Fig 10 is the direct evidence: in the solving baseline the encoder’s feature mean-cosine falls from 0.99 (states ~identical) toward 0.73 (states distinct) — and pairwise feature distance grows 26→65 — as eval success consolidates to 100%. So the random encoder is self-organising: it starts state-blind (good — undirected exploration, Fig 9 left), and the reward it stumbles onto is what carves the state structure it needs to exploit.

3.2 · Why doesn’t rescaling the JEPA features fix it? (it’s structure, not norm)

Rescaling cut the cumulative per-action advantage from 1.31 (raw) to 0.59 (norm-matched) — closer to random’s 0.41 — so it is tempting to think shrinking the features kills the phantom. It doesn’t, for a precise reason: the phantom comes from the feature directions (which states look different), and advantage normalization divides the magnitude back out. Rescaling can only weaken the signal’s consistency slightly; it cannot remove it. Fig 7 isolates this: with the JEPA encoder rescaled to the random encoder’s feature norm (≈2.3) and averaged over 40 independent random value heads, V(s) is still ~5× more spread than random’s (V_std 0.086±0.022 vs 0.017±0.003; bands disjoint). So the spread is created purely by the encoder’s structure, at matched magnitude and not from a lucky head.

4 · Causal confirmation: delete the critic, rescue the encoder

The mechanism makes a sharp prediction: if the value baseline is the source of the phantom gradient, then removing it — using Monte-Carlo advantages (advantage = discounted reward-to-go, which is exactly 0 until a real success) — should restore stable exploration for the JEPA encoder. It does, and reproducibly.

Robustness (seeds 0–2): “first-success update” (— = never)

conditionseed 0seed 1seed 2summary
JEPA enc + critic (resc_base)——581/3, and only late
random enc + critic (random_base)1862—2/3, fragile
JEPA enc, NO critic (resc_nobase)3424213/3, early

The value critic makes sparse-reward exploration fragile and seed-dependent for both encoders (the random encoder still has a small state-varying component, so it too occasionally manufactures enough phantom structure to fail — e.g. seed 2). Removing the critic makes the rich JEPA encoder the most reliable and fastest explorer. This is the within-encoder controlled result: resc_base vs resc_nobase differ only in the presence of the value baseline.

The right axis is critic vs no-critic, not encoder. It is tempting (and the seed-0 table in §2 invites it) to read this as “random encoder good, JEPA encoder bad.” That over-states it. The three regimes form a continuum in phantom-gradient strength: JEPA + critic = strong, state-consistent phantom (V_std≈5.5, −0.015 entropy/update) → reliably collapses; random + critic = weak phantom (V_std≈0.02, −0.0009/update) → behaves almost like pure random exploration but occasionally accumulates into a collapse (hence 2/3, fragile); JEPA + no critic = phantom is exactly 0 (the advantage is the reward-to-go, which is 0 until a real success) → genuinely pure max-entropy random exploration → reliably finds the reward, then learns. So “random + critic” and “JEPA + no critic” are indeed similar in spirit (both ≈ undirected exploration); they differ only in that the former carries a small destabilising critic term and the latter carries none. The encoder’s informativeness merely sets how strong the critic’s phantom signal is.

5 · The transfer twist (your Level-2 question)

Is a JEPA representation actually more transferable than a task-specific PPO one? We froze three encoders — random, JEPA-pretrained-on-L1, and the encoder of the PPO agent that solved L1 — and probed them on held-out Level-2 frames (reached via the engine set_level API) with two label-free read-outs: inverse-dynamics action decoding and forward-dynamics prediction.

Why the consensus (“self-supervised reps transfer better than task-specific RL reps”) holds — and where it breaks. It holds against the PPO encoder: maximizing a single task’s return is a compression pressure that discards everything not needed for that task’s reward, so the PPO-L1 encoder keeps L1-goal features and loses general dynamics — exactly what fails to transfer. The JEPA objective, by predicting the environment’s own dynamics, has no such pressure and preserves transferable structure. But it breaks in two honest ways here: (i) a random CNN transfers just as well as JEPA on these low-complexity ARC frames, so “learned SSL features” buy little over a random projection — the consensus is real but oversold at this scale; and (ii) — the central irony of this report — that same transferable richness is precisely what triggers the phantom-advantage trap. A representation’s mutual information with the latent state is simultaneously what makes it portable and what lets a critic hallucinate value structure before any reward exists.

6 · Takeaways

1. “Representation health” metrics (effective rank, feature diversity, world-model accuracy) do not predict RL usefulness: 10_2 had the highest effective rank and failed.   2. Under sparse reward, the diagnostic that matters is entropy stability before the first reward — if entropy falls with zero reward seen, the critic is hallucinating advantages.   3. The cheap fix is to silence the critic until the first reward (Monte-Carlo / no-baseline warm-up, or critic-free exploration), not to re-scale or freeze the encoder.   4. Transferability and RL-init quality can be anti-correlated: the better the world-model, the worse the cold-start explorer.

From repo root. Scripts in exp_010_3/scripts/, data in exp_010_3/data/, figures in exp_010_3/figures/.

Caveats: single game (LS20), Level 1→2 only, ≤3 seeds, 70–140 PPO updates per run; the L2 probe uses self-supervised read-outs, not end-to-end L2 solving (terminal-only PPO does not solve L2 from any init — an exploration limit, consistent with the phantom-advantage account). Conclusions are mechanistic and within-game; treat cross-game generality as a hypothesis.
